claims.claim: The Aragorn/Boromir/Elrond exchange is an English extraordinary for its simple timelessness that could not be mistaken for Capitol Hill, and Boromir's slight whine is characterising.
claims.source: Ursula K. Le Guin, From Elfland to Poughkeepsie (1973)
claims.quote: an English extraordinary for its simple timelessness

claims.claim: Le Guin's judgement that Tolkien's plain English is direct, concrete and simple is quoted and endorsed by a language blogger.
claims.quote: no ichor; everything is direct, concrete and simple
claims.page: 'How to see one's own world': Ursula K. Le Guin on writing style

claims.claim: Auden credits Tolkien with an amazing gift for naming and an exact eye for description that make the reader know the world like their own childhood.
claims.quote: a wonderfully exact eye for description
claims.page: W. H. Auden's 1954 review of The Fellowship of the Ring

claims.feature: names as prose beauty; historical density
claims.claim: Lewis calls the names a feast embodying piercing elvish beauty and says one cannot set foot anywhere without stirring the dust of history.
claims.source: C. S. Lewis, The Gods Return to Earth (TheOneRing reprint)
claims.quote: The names alone are a feast

claims.claim: Tolkien selects registers to suit peoples: simple and modern for hobbits, more archaic for Dwarves, Elves and Rohirrim, with hobbits mediating for the modern reader (Turner).
Shippey shows Elrond speaking with antique words and old-fashioned syntactic inversions while the hobbits speak modern English.
claims.quote: Now, therefore, things shall be openly spoken

claims.claim: Shippey reads Saruman's vocabulary as empty politician-speak built on words like 'real' and 'ultimate'.
claims.quote: we can bide our time, we can keep

claims.claim: Walker finds only a handful of genuinely archaic words, used rarely, yet the diction seems in essence nostalgic; the Riders of Rohan get Anglo-Saxon syntactic patterns and stately alliterative diction.
The repeated 'and' in the New Testament manner is stylistically marked, signalling something extraordinary (Turner/Shippey).

Rosebury answers Stimpson by showing that even her chosen example is as plain as Hemingway, and that the Merry/Witch-king passage begins plainly then modulates to a higher register for ancient history.
claims.quote: And still Meriadoc stood there blinking

claims.claim: Drout holds that the craftsmanship is consistent from the individual sentence to the macro-structure of the journey as a repeated stress-and-release pattern.
Walker's book argues the prose is strikingly invitational, taut with semantic ambiguity that widens meaning and draws the reader into sub-creation.
The ubi sunt theme gives elegiac tone and historical depth, as when Pippin guesses at great men and kindreds from the ruins.
claims.quote: Pippin guessed of great men and kindreds

claims.claim: The impression of depth is built from offhand, incomplete references to the past, multiple inconsistent accounts as in real history, and different texts written in different styles.
claims.source: Wikipedia, Impression of depth in The Lord of the Rings
claims.quote: from the Hoard of Scatha the Worm
claims.page: Impression of depth in The Lord of the Rings

claims.claim: Turner notes archaising object-fronting such as 'Weapons they have laid at your doors', which German can keep but French cannot render.
claims.source: Wikipedia, Translating The Lord of the Rings (Turner)
claims.quote: Weapons they have laid at your doors
claims.page: Translating The Lord of the Rings

verdicts.trueWording: an English extraordinary for its simple timelessness
verdicts.note: Le Guin PDF p.4-5, exact. Adjacent support: 'You could not possibly mistake them for anyone on Capitol Hill' (of all three passages) and 'the very slight whine in Boromir's tone is significant also... the flaw is envy'. Caveat: she also writes 'Such language is rare on Capitol Hill, but it has occurred there', so the Capitol Hill point is 'not mistakable for', not 'impossible there'.

verdicts.trueWording: he has no ichor; everything is direct, concrete and simple
verdicts.note: Exact inside Stan Carey's block quote of Le Guin's 'From Elfland to Poughkeepsie' (post dated 16 Oct 2024). 'Endorsed' is only implicit: Carey quotes approvingly and follows with his own plain-style paragraph, but never explicitly endorses the Tolkien judgement.

verdicts.trueWording: an amazing gift for naming and a wonderfully exact eye for description
verdicts.note: Exact on the LitHub reprint of Auden's 1954 review; the childhood clause follows verbatim: 'one knows the histories of Hobbits, Elves, Dwarves and the landscape they inhabit as well as one knows one's own childhood.'

verdicts.trueWording: The names alone are a feast
verdicts.note: Exact, continuing '... when they embody that piercing, high, elvish beauty of which no other prose writer has captured so much.' The second half of the claim is paraphrase: Lewis writes 'you can hardly put your foot down anywhere from Esgaroth to Forlindon... without stirring the dust of history' — 'set foot' is not his wording.

Exact in the lead. Attribution nuance: the lead says 'Commentators have noted'; the body section 'Hobbits as mediators with the heroic' does attribute the register contrast to Turner ('Turner states... Tolkien intentionally creates a contrast between the simple modern style of the Hobbits and more archaizing language for the Dwarves, Elves, and Riders of Rohan'), but the mediation point is footnoted to Shippey 2005 p.259, not Turner.

verdicts.trueWording: Now, therefore, things shall be openly spoken
verdicts.note: Exact; article gives the full sentence and attributes to Shippey 2005 pp.134-138: Elrond 'uses antique words like "esquire", "shards"... along with "old-fashioned inversions of syntax"'. The modern-hobbit contrast is supported in the same section (Gaffer/Sam) and the lead.

verdicts.trueWording: we can bide our time, we can keep
verdicts.note: Quote exact inside the Saruman block quote. Shippey's gloss is verified: 'no other character in the book uses words so empty of meaning as "real", "deploring", and "ultimate"'. But 'politician-speak' is the claim-writer's gloss — the word 'politic-' appears nowhere in the article; it says 'several modern evils'.

Exact (Walker 2009 p.143), as is the rest: 'only a few actually archaic words, and... Tolkien uses them only rarely'; the diction 'manages to seem in its essence nostalgic, maybe even archaic'; Rohan given 'Anglo-Saxon syntactic patterns'.

Exact in the Pelennor block quote. The observation is Turner's: paratactic 'and' 'in the manner of the New Testament' is 'stylistically marked', 'indicating something out of the ordinary'; Shippey is cited separately for 'loose semantic fit', so the Turner/Shippey joint attribution is loose but not wrong.

verdicts.trueWording: And still Meriadoc stood there blinking
verdicts.note: Exact. Lead confirms both halves: 'Where Stimpson called Tolkien's diction needlessly complex, Rosebury argues that even in the example she chose, Tolkien was as plain and simple as Ernest Hemingway... Tolkien begins this in plain language, modulating into a higher register to deal with the echoes of ancient and magical history.'

verdicts.trueWording: a repeated stress and release pattern
verdicts.note: Exact, but the framing is layered: the article says Le Guin argued this 'as Michael Drout writes', i.e. Drout is characterising Le Guin's 2001 account. 'Drout holds' is defensible only as Drout's own summary; the article's phrase is 'consistent at all levels of construction, from the individual sentence to the macro structure of the journey'.

Exact. Walker's own block quote supports the rest: 'His prose is taut with semantic ambiguities tending to widen potential meaning' and 'an open invitation to subcreation' (unhyphenated). Minor: the 'strikingly invitational' sentence is footnoted to West 2011, a review of Walker's book, not to Walker directly.

verdicts.trueWording: Pippin guessed of great men and kindreds
verdicts.note: Exact, in the Minas Tirith quotation. Walker 2009 p.85 is cited for the ubi sunt theme revisited 'usually with incidental casualness' 'to create an elegiac tone and a feeling of deep time and history behind what can be seen'.

verdicts.trueWording: from the Hoard of Scatha the Worm
verdicts.note: Exact. The four factors are listed verbatim: 'the apparently casual and incomplete mentions of this background'; 'multiple inconsistent accounts, as in real history'; 'writing different texts in varying styles' (body: 'as if by different hands'), all sourced to Drout, Hitotsubashi & Scavera 2014.

verdicts.trueWording: Weapons they have laid at your doors
verdicts.note: Exact. Article: 'Allan Turner gives the example of fronting, where Tolkien puts the object at the start of a sentence rather than after the verb... Turner points out that this cannot be done in French, while in German it remains a common construction and doesn't give an archaic effect.'
